title: AI Dominates Economy and Markets with Torsten Slok | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 68
summary: Slok attributes US resilience to AI spending, reshoring and tax refunds, while warning that higher rates and software refinancing challenge parts of private credit. Eisman questions AI moats and concentration. The interview separates aggregate consumer strength from lower-income stress, compares US and European dynamism, and explores Treasury-demand changes. Both end by warning that conventional portfolios contain more common AI exposure than investors may realize.
assessment: Full transcript reviewed. Empirical claims without inspected primary outcome evidence remain unresolved; guest claims are separate from Eisman attribution. Primary outcome verification is incomplete for claims marked unresolved; these are not adverse accuracy grades.
speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman is the host; Torsten Slok gives the macroeconomic answers. Closing remarks from 3198 onward are Eisman and explicitly adopt selected guest conclusions. Host questions and acknowledgments alone are not treated as endorsement.
framework_points: Decompose growth into drivers and identify which are rate-sensitive.
Separate sector credit distress from systemic leverage.
Evaluate refinancing risk with leverage, interest coverage, maturity and residual equity value.
Assess Treasury demand by investor type and maturity rather than deficit size alone.
tools_and_charts: New York Fed inflation by income
Credit default rates, distressed exchanges and liability-management exercises
Treasury holders, yield curve and fund flows
transcript_cautions: Slok's first growth estimate includes stock-market wealth effects, not solely direct AI capex; later shorthand risks losing that distinction.
Software maturity discussion specifies most refinancing in 2028-29 and only some in 2027.
The guest calls investment-grade indices partly government bonds, mixing corporate IG and broader fixed-income categories.
The 30,000 payroll breakeven is presented without the Dallas Fed's constant-participation assumption.
Captioned dollar values and immigration categories need source-definition checks.
